title: Drohiczyn’s Jewish community: life, work, and memory
summary: The memorial book’s central subject is the community itself, whose religious life, livelihoods, institutions, and fate are told across many accounts.
editorialContent:
![Drahichyn, the Belarusian town known in Yiddish as Drohitchin](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7d/Flag_of_Drahi%C4%8Dyn.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)
## A town remembered through its community

The Drohiczyn remembered in *Drohitchin: finf hundert yor Yidish-lebn*—“Five Hundred Years of Jewish Life”—is not simply a place where Jews lived. It is a network of homes, shops, study houses, religious obligations, livelihoods, political disagreements, and ties to nearby settlements. The book’s editors presented the community as a world that had been destroyed, but also as a world whose history and people deserved to be named and remembered. The [community commemorated by the volume](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_39d23dc1ff780fc5e0705ad8) is thus both the subject of a history and the object of a memorial.

The book itself cautions against treating its historical portrait as complete. Dov Warshavsky, writing about the town, said that the community’s *Pinkas*—its record book—had disappeared, and that he had no comprehensive historical documentation to rely on. He drew on childhood memories and the recollections of older residents. That candor matters: the book preserves the community’s own testimony, but its gaps are part of the story too.

## How large was the community?

The records provided from the book describe a community of considerable size, but do not give one consistent population figure. One account refers to [700 Jewish families](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_d9481e9c6be64d968eb9f144) before the war. The book’s broader memorial framing speaks of nearly five hundred years of Jewish life, while another description refers to the [Jewish residents whose population and livelihoods were discussed](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_ea295fe81894b5b0f5282a34). These figures may reflect different dates, definitions, or areas; the surviving descriptions do not allow them to be reconciled exactly.

An independent entry in Yad Vashem’s *Encyclopedia of the Ghettos* gives a different scale for the interwar years: approximately 1,500 Jews, around three-quarters of the town’s population. It also describes a community sustained largely by crafts and trade, especially commerce in agricultural produce. The difference between this estimate and the memorial book’s figure of 700 families should not be flattened into false precision. They may concern different time points or scopes, and the sources do not settle the question. ([Yad Vashem, “Drohiczyn”](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=257))

The community was connected to settlements beyond the town itself. The book’s record graph places [Yanave](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_dcceeb07f3d7101afef87785) and [Khamsk](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_b36c7a5729db693014cbb772) within Drohiczyn’s orbit, alongside Motele. Such connections help explain why “the community” could mean more than the residents of one built-up town: people, services, and communal relationships extended across the surrounding district.

## Work, learning, and mutual aid

Work shaped both household life and communal institutions. Yad Vashem’s account says that craftspeople and traders formed the backbone of interwar livelihoods, with agricultural produce an important part of commerce. It also notes a Jewish bank and a *Gemilut Hasadim* mutual-aid fund. The fund’s name appears among the book’s community connections as an institution located in Drohiczyn. Together, these details suggest an economic life in which private work and communal support were intertwined.

The book’s account of everyday geography gives this social world a physical centre. It remembers the synagogue courtyard as the spiritual hub and the market as the economic one: two centres around which the town’s Jewish life turned. A long main street linked these spaces with homes and shops. The description is a survivor’s reconstruction, not a town plan verified by independent records, but it conveys how residents understood their surroundings—not as separate “religious” and “commercial” worlds, but as connected parts of daily life.

Education and culture widened that world. Yad Vashem records a *Talmud Torah*, a Hebrew school associated with the Tarbut network, a branch of the Kultur-Lige, Hebrew and Yiddish books in the municipal library, and a drama circle. These institutions indicate that Jewish life in Drohiczyn was not only a matter of worship and trade. It also included modern Hebrew education, Yiddish cultural activity, reading, and performance. The memorial book’s contents list the [Bund](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_03cc6e293a8f8090e37f204a), one sign of the political diversity that existed alongside religious commitments.

## Religious character and communal institutions

The memorial book describes the community as mostly non-Hasidic, with a smaller Hasidic group. In the record graph, this appears as the claim that the [community was mostly Mitnagdim, with a Hasidic minority](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_b689953e52a7cfbbe5fa94d4). Warshavsky’s account adds texture: before the First World War, he recalled four study houses and a Hasidic *shtibl*. He said the community’s Hasidim followed the Kobrin tradition, while the majority prayed in the Ashkenazic rite. These are the book’s recollections; they should not be mistaken for a full census of religious affiliation.

Religious life also depended on practical institutions. The book remembers the *Chevra Kaddisha*, the burial society, as one of the community’s oldest bodies—and, under ghetto conditions, the only community institution still functioning officially until the Holocaust. Its lost record book, like the missing *Pinkas*, represents an archive of communal rules and events that did not survive. The account names rabbis and teachers, but admits that much about the town’s earlier religious leadership is unknown. Among the connected figures in the records are Rabbi Eliyahu Velvel Altvarg, who later settled in Drohiczyn, and the pious blacksmith Eliyahu Mordechai Levinowitz. Their presence hints at the range of people who shaped communal life, from formal religious leadership to religious practice embedded in ordinary work.

## Political upheaval and destruction

Drohiczyn’s Jewish life changed as borders and regimes changed. The independent record places the town in Poland between the wars and says Soviet forces occupied it in September 1939. Soviet rule brought the gradual elimination of private trade and craft work; a Yiddish school replaced the Hebrew school. Yad Vashem also records arrests and deportations of Jewish residents into the Soviet interior. This wider chronology adds political context that the memorial book’s memories alone cannot fully supply.

German forces entered the town in June 1941. Yad Vashem describes forced labour, a Jewish council, and two ghettos established in April 1942: one closed ghetto for workers deemed necessary and one open ghetto for others. It reports mass killings in July and October 1942, including the murder of about 1,500 people near the town in October. The memorial book remembers two massacres and commemorates thousands of victims; the sources differ in how they count victims and describe the sequence. Those differences should remain visible. They reflect distinct records and memorial purposes, not a reason to reduce the killing to a single uncontested number.

The book’s portrait of a community—its market, study houses, mutual aid, rabbis, schools, and political associations—cannot be separated from this destruction, but neither should it be reduced to it. The [German forces](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_4de741dc159f333c6f99f7a6) ended a civic world built over generations. The memorial volume, published in 1958, tried to restore some of that world in words: not as a complete archive, but as testimony to the people who had made Drohiczyn Jewish life meaningful.
